newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac denounces "conspiracy of silence" on Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Chirac denounces "conspiracy of silence" on Zaire.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, denouncing a "conspiracy of silence" on Zaire, appealed to the international community on Tuesday to force a ceasefire in the central African state and take emergency humanitarian action.

Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said Chirac told a cabinet meeting: "The humanitarian situation in Zaire is tragic. No one can ignore it any longer. No one can remain indifferent. We have to ask if there is not a sort of conspiracy of silence."

Ugandan-backed rebels fighting the government of autocratic French-backed President Mobutu Sese Seko have captured a swathe of eastern Zaire, driving Rwandan Hutu refugees before them, and threaten the key garrison city of Kisangani on the Zaire river.
Rebel leader Laurent-Desire Kabila has accepted a U.N. peace plan as a basis for talks but rejected its call for a ceasefire.

"France appeals solemnly to the international community to take responsibility by exerting the necessary pressure to obtain a ceasefire and to implement urgently needed humanitarian intervention," Chirac was quoted as saying.
He said Paris strongly backed proposals by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan for an international humanitarian intervention force, which the United States has rejected.

Emergency Humanitarian Aid Minister Xavier Emmanuelli, just back from Zaire, reported to the cabinet that the refugee situation was "very sombre" and proposed France launch its own mini-airlift while awaiting wider international support.

Military sources said France has only a small airlift capacity for long-range operations and no major international relief operation could be launched without U.S. help. This seemed unlikely unless American public opinion was to be swayed behind such a move.

"If we want the relief agencies to return (to Ubundu camp), we must guarantee security for these people and for the ferrying of relief supplies...I found a people in perdition, they are being chased and are losing the weak along the road," Emmanuelli told reporters.
He estimated that some 35,000 people had gathered there on the banks of the Zaire river, southeast of Kisangani.
"I heard eye-witness accounts of violence committed against them, of massacres. I cannot comment on them, I can only report them," he said.

Paris, warning of the dangers of a breakup of the giant central African state, has expressed mounting concern in the last week at anonymous reports of alleged massacres of Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire, angrily denied by the rebels.
Goma bishop Faustin Ngabu, president of the Zairean bishops' conference, denounced the reports as "partisan, dishonest and irresponsible".

"In a situation where rumour is the main source of information, it is easy to see mass graves everywhere...to decide from the outset that they are Hutu refugees, victims of Tutsi aggression," Ngabu, a Tutsi, said in a statement quoted by newspaper Le Monde.

Critics say France's humanitarian motives are suspect because it has long supported Mobutu, who is convalescing at his French Riviera villa after undergoing prostate cancer surgery in Switzerland last August.

Paris unofficially considers Zaire part of its private African "zone of influence" and believes it would be ejected from there, in favour of the United States, if Mobutu were to be overthrown by the rebels.

The rebels' radio said on Tuesday that the fall of Kisangani, the base for an ineffective mercenary-backed government counter-offensive, was imminent and repeated a March 13 deadline for Zaire army soldiers to give up their arms.
